### **Citywide Lead: World Series Championship Parade Rolls Through Downtown & Jack London Square**
**Oakland** enters **Cycle 111** under cold winter fog and gray marine skies, registering a triumphant reporting day anchored by the **Oakland Athletics' 7th World Series Championship Parade and Rally** [1, 3, 4]. Despite damp conditions, hundreds of thousands of fans packed Broadway and Jack London Square to celebrate the franchise's 7th title in the Mike Paulson era [4, 5].

* **The Double-Decker Victory Ride:** President of Baseball Operations **Mike Paulson**, retiring legends **Vinnie Keane** and **Benji Dillon**, and pending free agent **Mark Aitken** rode open-air double-decker buses through Downtown, waving to roaring crowds [4]. 
* **Clubhouse Celebrations:** Outfielders **Darrin Davis** and **Isley Kelley** celebrated along the route, while Manager **Deacon Seymour** and rookie phenom **Ernesto Quintero** tossed A's beads to fans [4]. Postseason and World Series MVP **Eric Taveras** (.339 AVG, 7 HR, 12 RBI in October) and ace **Arturo Ramos** took selfie snapshots and danced with supporters along the parade line [4, 5].
* **Offseason Roster Crossroads:** With the parade concluded, front-office focus turns immediately to crucial offseason decisions facing Mike Paulson [6]:
  * **First Base Transition:** Managing 33-year-old franchise icon **Mark Aitken’s** pending free agency, with rising slugger **Ernesto Quintero** potentially moving to first base to open everyday at-bats for **Kevin Clark** [6].
  * **Rotation & Outfield Battles:** Rookie **Pablo Almanzar** has cemented his starting rotation spot alongside Arturo Ramos, Travis Coles, and John Ellis, leaving **Carmen Mesa** facing a AAA assignment or trade [5, 6]. In the outfield, **Desmond Morton** and **Frank Reyna** will compete for the remaining everyday outfield slot [6].
  * **Bullpen Refresh:** Front-office analysts are targeting high-end relief depth after late-postseason bullpen fatigue [6].

### **The Gate Desk**

The editorial board has audited the single gate-flagged reporter draft submitted in the source database for Cycle 111. Below is the complete accounting of what the draft reported, what the editorial gate uncovered, and how those findings hold up against verified world records:

#### **1. `West Oakland's Month-Ten Money Clears the Desk. What Happens on the Street Is Not on the Ledger.`**
* **What the Draft Reported:**  
  This civic affairs draft reported on Month 10 of the West Oakland Stabilization Fund (\$400,000 approved, \$22.6 million remaining in the envelope) [15, 16]. It quoted claims by Finance Committee official **Marcus Webb** that 91 West Oakland households were stabilized with full compliance standards that will survive audit [40]. It also cited Mayor Avery Santana, Councilmember Denise Carter, and Executive Leadership official Brenda Okoro arguing that direct payments are outpacing displacement [15, 18].
* **What the Gate Found:**  
  The editorial gate flagged and held back this draft from publication [15]. The gate identified unverified audit claims and a household count discrepancy: the draft asserted audit compliance before an official audit was published and cited Webb's claim of 91 stabilized households, whereas official ledger records in Cycle 110 logged 79 stabilized households [14, 15, 40].
* **Whether the Finding Holds Up Against Other Sources:**  
  **Yes, the gate's decision holds up completely.** Official records in the `Initiative_Tracker` confirm \$22.6 million remaining and 79 households stabilized through Month 9 [14]. Webb's claim of 91 households represented an unverified projection rather than a reconciled ledger fact, and claiming audit compliance before an official audit report was published violated strict newsroom verification standards [14, 40].

In West Oakland, the Stabilization Fund's latest payment is a number on a page before it is anything else: $400,000, approved for month ten. Mayor Avery Santana's office put the families at the center of it in its own record: "The families who qualified for this money six months ago shouldn't wait another day — month-ten disbursement is approved."

Six months is the gap the Mayor named. The ledger shows the money moving in the other direction, through a schedule that is already set. The program carries a $28,000,000 budget. The tracker shows $22,600,000 remaining and records Cycle 111 as the last disbursement. The Cycle 110 payment was the month-nine disbursement of $400K, and the tracker logged a 23-day average processing time that cycle. This cycle the record reports the 23-day processing standard maintained. That is the first clock the fund keeps, and it is the one the office most readily reports.

Brenda Okoro's office record offers the sharpest frame for the pace: "Stabilization is a race against displacement — month-ten disbursement keeps us ahead." Ahead of what is the open question. The packet records payment timing and processing speed. It does not record whether any household's housing outcome changed after a payment.

The Port's growth and revenue uptick are notable, but I want to dig into what that means for the workers on the ground. The Port Got Louder. Down the Block, the Ledger Barely Moved. Developing report — edited but not yet published. The Port Got Louder. Down the Block, the Ledger Barely Moved. By Jordan Velez, Business Reporter Elle Lilo still spends her shifts doing what she has always done at the Port of Oakland: bringing ships in. She is a harbor tugboat captain, one of 1,501 people on the Port's payroll this cycle. The Port's books grew by $765,000 since last cycle, to $425.1 million. On the water, Lilo says, the difference is mostly the volume of the noise.

Now walk inland from the water to the neighborhood's dining rooms and bar rails. That is where a port's growth is supposed to spill over: the crew grabbing a plate after a double, the warehouse worker stopping for a drink. Green & Gold Tavern carries 30 workers, among them dishwasher Hector Leech, servers Trenton Nawan and Valentina Campbell, and bartender Guadalupe Lupe. The tavern's revenue rose $6,000 since last cycle, to $3.7 million. Blue Lantern Bar, where Yuki Ji and Guadalupe Lee pour, also employs 30 and added $7,000, to $3.9 million. Harborline Grill is a seven-person kitchen whose line includes Tomas Renteria, Quynh Le, Jalen Hill and Bruce Wright. It brought in $1,000 more than last cycle, for $860,000 total.

East Oakland follows at 123, Ivy Hill at 122, and Fruitvale at 118. Across 22 neighborhoods the total is 1,907. Chinatown's 144 comes to 6.6 percent of its 2,193 residents, at or above the 6 percent watch bar the record sets. Then the record turns to the hospital, and the count gets smaller. Chinatown produced 3 admissions this cycle. At the close, 6 Chinatown residents were in care, occupying 6 beds. The census counts all six as other residents, with none tracked by name. Citywide, the hospital took 37 admissions, held 75 in care at the close, and filled 75 beds. Thirty-nine residents left care during the cycle.

Chinatown's Line Is Shorter Than Its Count Developing report — edited but not yet published. Chinatown's Line Is Shorter Than Its Count By Dr. Lila Mezran Mai Tse walks to school past the line every morning. She is a student in Chinatown, and she has a view of the clinic that most people in the city would not get. "I see the clinic lines every morning when I walk to school," she says. "Mostly, it's older people who go in, and sometimes parents with little kids. I don't see many people my age there. Some people wait for a while, but others just look at the line and walk away. I don't know why they leave—maybe it's too long, or they don't think they need it."

The clinic is the community clinic on 8th Street. Niani Oakley, a plumber who lives in Chinatown, knows it the way neighbors know a corner store. She describes the place as a first stop, not a last one. "Most folks around here, if it's not an emergency but they need more than home remedies, they'll head over to the community clinic on 8th Street. It's close, and they know how to handle the usual stuff without making a big deal out of it." Those two accounts, a student watching from the sidewalk and a tradesperson who knows the block, are the closest thing this cycle's record offers to a view from the street. The rest of the record is in numbers, and the numbers say Chinatown is carrying more illness than any other neighborhood in the city.

12th St Oakland City Center ridership down 15,192 vs C110 | 8 stations + 10 corridors on the record — the platforms and the people who run them Trevor Shimizu: Trevor's chasing the quiet story behind the numbers—why 12th Street's platforms felt emptier even as on-time performance ticked up. He wants to stand at the fare gates during the 7:40am surge and listen to what regulars complain about. The holiday dip is obvious, but something about the Baylight District construction vote doesn't add up—if it's 'construction-active,' where are the workers?

The question this cycle's record leaves open is when recovering at home stops being a choice a household makes and becomes something the system has stopped tracking. Who should answer that, and how the city would know which residents are on the far side of that line, the record does not say. 12th Street Is Running Better. The People Are Somewhere Else. Developing report — edited but not yet published. 12th Street Is Running Better. The People Are Somewhere Else. By Trevor Shimizu At 7:40 at 12th St Oakland City Center, Joel Wren was looking at a quieter station and a smoother service. The station recorded 8,293 riders in Cycle 111, down 15,192 from the previous cycle. Its on-time performance improved to 86%, five points higher than before.

Those two measurements are supposed to describe the same transit system. Here they do not. “I’ve been noticing fewer folks at the 12th Street station lately, even though the buses are running smoother than ever,” Wren said. “It’s strange—people used to pack in there, but now it feels quieter. Maybe it’s the Baylight construction approvals making folks rethink their routes. Hard to say, but something’s shifted.” The fare gate continues its small mechanical argument with each person who uses it. The schedule can be better while the station becomes less useful. On-time performance measures whether service arrives when expected. Ridership measures whether people still choose to be there. A system can improve the first measure and lose the second.

The infrastructure question is therefore not only whether a bus arrives on time. It is whether the full path to the bus remains attractive enough to use. Cycle 111 shows a service that is, in several places, more punctual and less occupied. Before Baylight District construction advances further, the unanswered maintenance question is simple: where did the 15,192 missing 12th Street riders go?
